lessons.title: Why indemnification is the hardest part of a deal to picture

blocks.markdown:
Most people who negotiate indemnification clauses have never watched one operate.

That is not a criticism. It is structural. Claims are rare relative to deals. A dealmaker might close twenty agreements and see a single third-party claim arise from any of them. And when that claim does arrive, it usually lands on a different desk. Litigation counsel takes the file. The person who negotiated the cap three years earlier rarely learns whether the number they fought for mattered.

The result is a strange asymmetry. Indemnity language is among the most heavily negotiated parts of an agreement, and among the parts whose real-world operation is least understood by the people negotiating it.

Reading an indemnification clause tells you what it says. It does not tell you what happens in month seven, when the claim is live, the parties disagree about whether to settle, and the insurer has just sent a reservation of rights letter.

## The spine of this module

This module is built around that gap. Its spine is the third-party claim lifecycle: a letter arrives, notice gets given, someone takes control of the defense, the parties argue about settlement, and eventually money moves — or doesn't.

Everything else you will meet here — representations, warranties, caps, baskets, survival periods, escrow, insurance — is taught as machinery that determines how that lifecycle plays out.

That reframing matters more than it might sound.

A cap is not an abstract number. It is the point at which the indemnifying party stops caring about the outcome of a litigation they may still be controlling. A survival period is not a date. It is the moment a problem you have not yet discovered becomes permanently yours. A consent-to-settle provision is not a formality. It is the mechanism that decides who wins an argument the parties are certain to have.

## One thing worth naming early

A large part of indemnity negotiation is not really about indemnity. It is about price.

When a buyer pushes the cap from ten per cent of deal value to twenty, they are buying something. The seller is selling it. The parties are allocating residual risk, and residual risk has a value that could in principle be reflected in the headline number instead.

Treating the negotiation as a purely legal argument, rather than a commercial one with legal vocabulary, is a common way to lose it.

## What this module does not do

It does not teach you to draft. It does not substitute for counsel — and where a point turns on the law of a particular jurisdiction, that will be said plainly rather than buried.

What it should do is let you sit in a negotiation, or in the first meeting after a claim letter arrives, and understand what the package in front of you actually does under stress.

questions.stem: Why is the operation of an indemnity clause typically invisible to the person who negotiated it?
options: Indemnity clauses are rarely enforced in commercial practice
Claims are rare relative to deals, and when they arise they are usually handled by different people
Confidentiality provisions prevent dealmakers from learning claim outcomes
Indemnity obligations are usually settled before any procedure is triggered
questions.explanation: The gap is structural rather than legal. A dealmaker closes many agreements and sees few claims, and when a claim does arise the file typically moves to litigation counsel. The negotiator seldom learns how their drafting choices performed.

lessons.title: Representations and warranties: the foundation indemnity sits on

blocks.markdown:
Almost every indemnification claim begins in the same place: someone said something that turned out not to be true.

That makes representations and warranties the foundation the whole indemnity package rests on. Understanding what they are — and more importantly, what qualifies them — determines how much protection the indemnity actually provides.

## Three words that are not interchangeable

A **representation** is a statement of fact about the present or the past. The seller represents that it owns the assets, that the regulatory filings are accurate, that there is no pending litigation beyond what has been disclosed.

A **warranty** is a promise that the statement is true, carrying a remedy if it is not.

A **covenant** is different in kind: a promise to do, or refrain from doing, something going forward. Operating the business in the ordinary course between signing and closing is a covenant, not a representation.

In practice, commercial agreements bundle the first two into a single formula — *represents and warrants* — and in most civil law jurisdictions the distinction carries little practical consequence.

Under English and US law it historically mattered. A false representation could support rescission or a claim in tort; a breached warranty gave contract damages. The combined formula survives partly out of caution and partly out of habit. It is worth knowing that the two words are doing different historical work, even where a court will treat them as one.

## Two words that can gut a representation

*To the seller's knowledge.*

A knowledge qualifier converts a promise that something is true into a promise that the seller is not aware it is false. Everything the seller genuinely did not know becomes the buyer's problem.

This is not a drafting nicety. It is one of the largest risk transfers available in a commercial agreement, and it is accomplished in four words.

Three questions decide how much a knowledge qualifier costs:

- **Whose knowledge counts?** The company's? Named individuals'? Anyone in management?
- **Actual or constructive?** Does it mean what the seller genuinely knew, or also what a reasonable enquiry would have surfaced?
- **Is it defined at all?** An unqualified reference to "knowledge" with no definition is an invitation to argue about it later, at a point when both sides have strong incentives to remember things differently.

A defined knowledge standard naming specific individuals and specifying actual versus constructive awareness is worth more than an extra few percentage points on the cap.

## Materiality, and scraping it out

*In all material respects* does similar work from a different angle. It excuses small inaccuracies, and shifts the argument to whether a given inaccuracy was small.

Which is why the **materiality scrape** exists. A scrape instructs the reader to ignore materiality qualifiers when calculating losses — so once a breach is established, damages are measured on the full amount rather than only the portion above the materiality line.

A **double materiality scrape** goes further and removes materiality for determining whether a breach occurred at all, not merely for quantifying it. The difference between the two is frequently glossed over in negotiation and is not small.

## Where a great deal of real risk allocation actually happens

Then there are the disclosure schedules.

Anything properly disclosed against a representation is carved out of it. The seller is not in breach of a representation about pending litigation for the litigation it listed. Schedules are, in substance, a second negotiation about risk — conducted in a spreadsheet.

They are also usually assembled late, under time pressure, and with less senior attention than the clause language received. A sophisticated buyer reads the schedules at least as carefully as the reps. Many do not.

cards.back: A statement of fact about the present or the past — that the assets are owned, the filings are accurate, the disclosed litigation is complete.
A promise that a statement is true, carrying a remedy if it is not. Usually bundled with representation as 'represents and warrants'.
A promise to do or not do something going forward — different in kind from a representation, which looks backward or at the present.
Language ('to the seller's knowledge') converting a promise that something is true into a promise that the seller is unaware it is false. Shifts unknown risk to the buyer.
A provision reading materiality qualifiers out when calculating losses. A double scrape also removes them when determining whether a breach occurred.

questions.stem: What is the practical effect of a knowledge qualifier on a representation?
options: It limits the amount recoverable for breach of that representation
It shortens the period during which the representation survives
It shifts the risk of matters the seller did not know about onto the buyer
It requires the buyer to conduct independent verification before closing
questions.explanation: A knowledge qualifier changes the promise from 'this is true' to 'I am not aware this is false'. Anything the seller genuinely did not know falls outside the representation and therefore outside the indemnity that rests on it.

blocks.markdown:
An indemnification regime answers six questions. They are worth separating, because they are negotiated on different logic and they fail in different ways.

- Who indemnifies whom
- For what losses
- Triggered by what
- Subject to what procedure
- Limited how
- To the exclusion of what other remedies

Most of this module deals with the fourth and fifth. This lesson covers the rest.

## Indemnify, defend, hold harmless

These three appear together so often that they read as a single incantation. They are not the same thing.

**Indemnify** means reimburse for losses suffered. It operates after the fact.

**Defend** is an obligation that arises earlier and is often broader: a duty to take on and fund the defense of a claim from the moment it is asserted, regardless of whether it eventually proves meritorious. A party can owe a defense on a claim it ultimately owes no indemnity on — the claim fails, but the defense still had to be paid for while it was live.

**Hold harmless** is treated by many courts as synonymous with indemnify. It is sometimes argued to be broader: protection from liability arising at all, rather than reimbursement once it has. The argument is worth knowing even where a court collapses the two.

attributes.label: When it arises
values: After liability is established — reimburses losses already suffered
When the claim is asserted, not when it is proven
Often treated as synonymous with indemnify; sometimes argued to prevent liability arising at all

attributes.label: Owed even if claim fails?
values: No — owed only where the indemnity is actually triggered
Yes — defense costs accrue while the claim is live regardless of outcome
Depends on how the court reads it; worth reading carefully rather than assuming it is filler

blocks.markdown:
## What counts as a loss

The definition of covered losses is where a surprising amount of value sits, and it is often skimmed because it looks like boilerplate.

Does it include legal fees and the costs of investigation? Fees incurred in pursuing the indemnity claim itself, as opposed to defending the underlying claim? Amounts paid in settlement, and if so, settlements entered into without the indemnifying party's consent? Diminution in value of the acquired business, or only out-of-pocket amounts?

Each of these is a live negotiation point dressed as a definition.

## Triggers

Most indemnities are triggered by one of three things: breach of a representation or warranty, breach of a covenant, or a specifically identified matter.

The first is the most common and is the reason the previous lesson spent its time on qualifiers. The second is usually less contested. The third deserves its own paragraph.

## Specific indemnities

Some risks are known to both parties at signing. Litigation already filed. A regulatory question already under discussion with an agency. A recall in progress. An environmental liability at a manufacturing site.

These are commonly pulled out of the general regime and given their own indemnity — and they typically sit outside the cap, outside the basket, and sometimes outside the survival period.

The logic is clean once stated. The general regime allocates *unknown* risk, and its limits are priced accordingly. A specific indemnity allocates a risk both parties can name and size. There is no reason to make a known liability compete with unknown ones for room under a shared cap.

## Exclusive remedy

Most well-constructed indemnity regimes include an exclusive remedy provision: indemnification is the sole recourse for breaches of the agreement, to the exclusion of other contractual or tortious claims.

Without it, the carefully negotiated caps, baskets and survival periods can be circumvented by pleading the same facts as misrepresentation or negligence and escaping the limits entirely.

The carve-out is almost always fraud. The scope of that carve-out repays careful reading, because 'fraud' can be defined narrowly enough to be nearly unreachable, or broadly enough to swallow the exclusivity it is carved out of.

cards.back: Indemnify reimburses losses after the fact. Defend funds the defense from the moment a claim is asserted — and can be owed on claims that ultimately fail.
An indemnity for a known, identified risk (pending litigation, a live regulatory issue). Usually sits outside the cap, basket and sometimes the survival period.
Makes indemnification the sole recourse for breach, preventing the negotiated limits from being circumvented by tort or misrepresentation claims. Almost always carves out fraud.

questions.stem: Why do specific indemnities typically sit outside the general cap and basket?
options: Because they are usually smaller than general indemnity claims
Because the general regime prices unknown risk, while a specific indemnity covers a risk both parties can already name and size
Because they are governed by different law than the rest of the agreement
Because insurers require known liabilities to be separately stated
questions.explanation: The general regime's limits are calibrated to unknown risk. A liability both parties can identify and quantify at signing has no reason to compete for room under a cap priced for uncertainty.

lessons.title: Direct claims and third-party claims: two different machines

blocks.markdown:
There are two fundamentally different ways an indemnity gets called on, and agreements routinely blur them.

A **direct claim** is one party to the agreement claiming against the other. The buyer discovers after closing that a representation was false, and claims against the seller. Nobody from outside is involved.

A **third-party claim** is an outside party — a patient, a regulator, a competitor, a tax authority — asserting a claim against the indemnified party, with the indemnifying party on the hook for the consequences.

## Why the procedures diverge sharply

In a direct claim there is nothing to defend. No external proceeding, no outside claimant, no real-time decisions. The procedure is simply: notice, a response period, and then whatever dispute resolution mechanism the agreement provides. The entire question is whether the indemnity is owed.

In a third-party claim there is a live proceeding that somebody has to run. Counsel must be instructed. Filings have deadlines. Settlement offers arrive and expire. Decisions must be made continuously, by someone, while the parties may disagree about what those decisions should be.

That is why the third-party machinery exists: notice requirements, control of defense, cooperation duties, consent to settle. None of it has any application to a direct claim.

attributes.label: Who is claiming
values: One party to the agreement against the other
An outside party against the indemnified party

attributes.label: Is there a defense to run?
values: A live proceeding someone must run in real time

attributes.label: Procedure
values: Notice, control of defense, cooperation, consent to settle

attributes.label: What is in issue
values: Only whether the indemnity is owed
Both whether the indemnity is owed and how the claim is handled

blocks.markdown:
## Where agreements get this wrong

Three failure patterns show up repeatedly.

The first is a single combined procedure. The agreement defines "Claim" once and applies one set of mechanics to everything, producing provisions that make no sense when read against a direct claim. Who assumes the defense of a claim that has no defense?

The second is the opposite: elaborate third-party machinery and no direct claim procedure at all. The buyer discovers a breach and finds the agreement silent on how to assert it — what notice is required, what the seller's response window is, what happens if the seller simply does not reply.

The third is subtler. Direct claim notice requirements are often borrowed from the third-party section without adjustment, importing conditions that are natural for an external claim and difficult for an internal one.

## The notice trap in direct claims

This is where direct claims most often die.

A typical provision requires notice specifying the basis for the claim, the representation alleged to have been breached, and a good-faith estimate of the loss. That last requirement is the problem. A buyer can discover in month twenty that something is wrong, know it is a breach, and be genuinely unable to quantify it — because the investigation is ongoing, or because the loss depends on a regulatory outcome that will not arrive for another year.

If the survival period ends at month twenty-four, the buyer is forced to choose between a notice that may be attacked as deficient and no notice at all.

The practical answer, negotiated in advance, is language permitting notice of a claim with an estimate "to the extent then determinable," preserving the claim without demanding a number that does not yet exist.

## One set of facts, both claim types

The two are not mutually exclusive, and in pharma they frequently arrive together.

A patient brings a product liability claim against the acquired business. That is a third-party claim, and the third-party procedure governs how it is defended. But the fact that the seller knew of the safety signal and did not disclose it is also a breach of a representation — a direct claim, with its own notice requirement and its own path.

The same facts, two procedures, two sets of deadlines, and a real risk that satisfying one while overlooking the other leaves part of the exposure unrecovered.

cards.back: A claim by one party to the agreement against the other, with no outside claimant. No defense to control — the only question is whether the indemnity is owed.
A claim by an outside party against the indemnified party, with the indemnifying party on the hook. Requires real-time defense decisions, hence the procedural machinery.

questions.stem: Why do third-party claims require procedural provisions that direct claims do not?
options: Third-party claims are typically larger in value
A third-party claim involves a live external proceeding requiring continuous real-time decisions by someone
Direct claims are usually resolved before any procedure applies
Insurers only require notice for third-party claims
questions.explanation: A third-party claim means an outside proceeding that must actually be run — counsel instructed, deadlines met, settlement offers answered. Control, cooperation and consent-to-settle provisions exist to decide who makes those calls. A direct claim has no defense to conduct.

lessons.title: A third-party claim arrives: the first thirty days

blocks.markdown:
A letter arrives. A regulator opens an inquiry. A competitor files. Whatever the form, the clock has started, and several clocks have started at once.

The first weeks after a claim surfaces determine a surprising amount of what follows. Not because the legal merits change, but because the procedural and coverage positions can be permanently damaged in that window — quietly, by people acting reasonably.

## What the notice provision actually requires

Read it for three things.

**Timing.** "Promptly," "as soon as reasonably practicable," or a specific number of days. The vaguer formulations are more forgiving in principle and more arguable in practice.

**Content.** A description of the claim, the basis on which indemnification is sought, copies of the claim documents, and often an estimate of the loss. Notice that omits a required element can be attacked as defective even when it arrived on time.

**Consequence.** This is the one people skip. Does the agreement say notice is a *condition precedent* to indemnification?

## The prejudice question

Under most commercial law, late notice defeats an indemnity claim only to the extent the indemnifying party was actually prejudiced by the delay. If they lost the ability to defend effectively, the argument bites. If they lost nothing, courts are generally reluctant to void the indemnity over a procedural slip.

That comfortable position weakens considerably where the agreement makes notice an express condition precedent. Then the failure is not a breach to be measured — it is an unmet condition, and the obligation may never arise at all.

The word to search for is *condition*. It changes the risk profile of a missed deadline from arguable to fatal.

## Two clocks, not one

Here is the failure that quietly destroys more value than any drafting error.

The contractual notice goes to the indemnifying party. A separate notice is owed to the insurer under the policy. They run on **different deadlines with different requirements**, and the insurance clock is the less forgiving of the two.

Late notice to a counterparty is usually met with the prejudice argument above. Late notice to an insurer can eliminate coverage outright. Under a **claims-made** policy, notice within the policy period is not merely a procedural step — it is what triggers coverage to exist at all.

The pattern is familiar and entirely avoidable: legal notifies the counterparty within the contractual window, the broker is told weeks later once the matter feels serious, and the policy that would have covered the loss is no longer available.

events.title: The claim surfaces
events.description: Before anything else: do not respond substantively to the claimant.

events.title: Preserve and calendar
events.description: Issue a litigation hold and preserve documents. Calendar every contractual and policy deadline.

events.title: Notify the insurer
events.description: Notify the insurer and the broker. This clock is stricter than the contractual one and is the easiest to lose.

events.title: Assess the claim
events.description: Assess whether the claim is genuinely indemnifiable, and under which provision. Identify which policies are in play.

events.title: Serve contractual notice
events.description: Serve contractual notice containing every element the provision requires, not merely a heads-up.

events.title: The election window opens
events.description: The indemnifying party's election window to assume the defense begins. Lesson 6 covers what happens next.

blocks.markdown:
## The litigation hold

One item on that list deserves separating out, because it is the one most often handled badly by people who have never done it.

When a claim becomes reasonably foreseeable, the duty to preserve relevant documents attaches. Routine deletion policies must be suspended for anything within scope. Custodians must be identified and instructed.

Get this wrong and the consequences are not confined to the underlying claim. Spoliation findings travel: adverse inferences, sanctions, and a defense conducted from a materially weaker position regardless of the merits. It is also the kind of failure that makes an indemnifying party genuinely prejudiced by your handling of the matter — which is precisely the argument that converts a technical notice defect into a real one.

## What not to do

Do not engage substantively with the claimant before internal alignment. A well-intentioned reply acknowledging facts, offering an explanation, or proposing a commercial resolution can prejudice the defense and complicate coverage before anyone with responsibility for either has seen the file.

And do not wait for certainty before notifying. Both the contractual and policy notice provisions are generally satisfied by notifying a claim that *may* give rise to liability. Waiting until the position is clear is how deadlines are missed.

cards.back: Language making notice a precondition to the indemnity obligation arising at all. Converts a missed deadline from an arguable breach into a potentially fatal failure.
A policy where notice within the policy period is what triggers coverage to exist. Late notice does not merely weaken the claim — it can eliminate coverage.
Suspension of routine document deletion once a claim becomes reasonably foreseeable. Failure can produce spoliation sanctions independent of the claim's merits.

questions.stem: Why is late notice to an insurer generally more damaging than late notice to the indemnifying party?
options: Insurance policies carry statutory notice deadlines that contracts cannot vary
Insurers are not subject to the prejudice analysis that usually softens late contractual notice, and under a claims-made policy timely notice is what creates coverage at all
Contractual notice deadlines are generally longer than policy deadlines
Insurers cannot decline coverage once a claim has been asserted
questions.explanation: Late contractual notice is usually measured against actual prejudice to the indemnifying party. Policy notice is treated far more strictly, and with a claims-made policy notice inside the period is the event that brings coverage into existence.

lessons.title: Control of defense: who runs the litigation

blocks.markdown:
Control of defense is the most consequential procedural term in an indemnity package and the one least likely to be argued about at signing.

It decides who selects counsel, who sets strategy, who decides what to concede, and whose judgment governs when a settlement offer lands. It determines, in practice, whether the litigation is run to minimise payout or run to protect a business.

## Why each side wants it

The **indemnifying party** wants control because they are paying. Their concern is straightforward and legitimate: a party defending a claim with someone else's money has weak incentives to defend economically. Every hour of senior counsel, every expert retained, every motion filed is billed to a payer with no say.

The **indemnified party** resists because the claim is happening to their business. They still sell the product. They still have the regulatory relationship. They will still be operating in that market long after the file closes.

A defense optimised to minimise a payment is not the same defense as one optimised to protect a franchise. A settlement carrying an admission, or a public filing making a damaging concession on a scientific point, may be an excellent outcome for the payer and a serious problem for the operator.

## The mechanics

Most regimes follow the same shape.

Following notice, the indemnifying party has a defined window — commonly fifteen to thirty days — to **elect to assume the defense**. Silence is usually treated as declining.

If they assume it, counsel is typically required to be *reasonably satisfactory to* the indemnified party. That phrase is doing real work and is worth negotiating rather than accepting as boilerplate.

The indemnified party normally retains a right to **participate at its own expense** — to have its own counsel monitor, attend, and be consulted, without controlling.

If the indemnifying party declines or fails to elect, the indemnified party defends, and can generally recover reasonable defense costs as part of the indemnified loss.

## The carve-outs that shift control back

A well-drafted clause returns control to the indemnified party in defined circumstances. These are the ones worth insisting on.

**Conflict of interest.** Where the parties' interests in the defense genuinely diverge, common counsel is untenable.

**Non-monetary relief.** Where the claim seeks an injunction, or anything that would constrain how the business operates, the party that has to live with the outcome should be running it.

**Criminal or regulatory proceedings.** Different stakes, different consequences, and an exposure that does not end with a payment.

**Claims exceeding the cap.** This one is the sharpest and the most frequently omitted. If the claim is worth more than the indemnifying party's remaining exposure under the cap, the economics invert. They are now controlling a litigation whose downside above the cap falls entirely on someone else — and their incentive to fight it hard disappears at precisely the point the other party's exposure begins.

## Where an insurer is involved, control is a three-way question

The contract allocates control between two parties. The policy may allocate it to a third.

Many liability policies give the insurer the right to appoint counsel, frequently from a **panel** of firms with pre-agreed rates. Where the insurer is funding the defense, that right can in practice override what the parties negotiated between themselves. The agreement says the indemnifying party controls and selects counsel reasonably satisfactory to the other side; the policy says the insurer appoints from its panel. The policy is paying.

This is not hypothetical. It surfaces in the first weeks of a covered claim, and it surprises people who negotiated the contract carefully and never read the policy.

## Defending under a reservation of rights

A further wrinkle, and an uncomfortable one.

An insurer will often fund a defense while **reserving its rights** — preserving the ability to deny coverage later, once the facts develop. The defense proceeds. The bills are paid. And the insurer retains the option to conclude that the matter was never covered.

This puts appointed counsel in a structurally awkward position. They are defending the insured, but were selected by, and are reporting to, a party that may ultimately be adverse to the insured on coverage. Facts developed in the defense can inform the coverage decision.

Where the conflict is material, some jurisdictions give the insured a right to **independent counsel** at the insurer's expense. Whether that right exists, and what triggers it, is jurisdiction-specific — consult qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction. What is not jurisdiction-specific is the need to notice the problem early rather than discovering it in month nine.

cards.back: The indemnifying party's defined window after notice — commonly 15-30 days — to take control of defending a third-party claim. Silence usually counts as declining.
Law firms an insurer appoints from at pre-agreed rates. Where the insurer funds the defense, this right can override the counsel-selection terms the parties negotiated.
An insurer funding a defense while preserving its ability to deny coverage later. Creates a structural conflict for insurer-appointed counsel.

questions.stem: Why should control of defense shift to the indemnified party when a claim exceeds the cap?
options: Because the indemnifying party's insurance will not respond above the cap
Because the indemnifying party would be controlling a litigation whose exposure above the cap falls entirely on the other party, removing their incentive to defend it hard
Because caps are unenforceable once a claim exceeds them
Because the indemnified party is better placed to negotiate a settlement
questions.explanation: Above the cap, the indemnifying party has no remaining financial stake. They are running a defense where every additional unit of liability lands on someone else — exactly the misalignment the carve-out exists to prevent.
